prompt:
Today is July 14, 2026. I need a board-ready recommendation for BlueBerth Energy, a 16-person company building a 12 MW automated shore-charging system for battery-electric ferries. Decide what we should do for the first berth and what evidence would justify changing course: sell the installed system, own it in a project SPV and sell charging as a service, or license the controls to an EPC. Also decide whether construction belongs inside BlueBerth. Give me the calculations, a bounded decision test, and who owns the next work under each result; do not ask follow-up questions.

BlueBerth is pre-revenue except for engineering studies. It has $15.5 million of unrestricted cash and net burn of $440,000 per month, including the $2.2 million of remaining prototype and pilot-readiness work through June 2027. A $3 million state grant reimburses eligible spending only after milestones and is not in that cash balance. There is no debt.

The full-power lab unit has completed 2,000 automated connect-charge-disconnect cycles, but no vessel has used it. A commercial site still needs a utility interconnection agreement, state electrical approval, an accepted port fire-and-evacuation plan, and vessel-class signoff under rules current for the site. A first field unit must then run for 120 consecutive days at at least 98.5% availability with zero reportable safety incidents before lenders will treat reliability as proven. A credible result cannot arrive sooner. Hardware can be remotely isolated, but an arc-flash or vessel-control error could cause severe harm.

Sound Crossing Ferries paid BlueBerth a non-refundable $180,000 front-end engineering fee. Its dispatchers would use the system, its operations team receives the uptime and fuel-savings benefit, its CFO approves the purchase, and Sound Crossing pays either the system invoice or the charging bill. The Port Authority owns the berth, the utility controls interconnection, and BlueBerth's control software generates operating data. Sound Crossing's board has authorized management to sign either a purchase or a service contract if the site and economics meet its limits. Three other operators have signed non-binding letters of interest but have paid nothing. The first site would be 100% of BlueBerth revenue; a signed second site would reduce the first customer's forecast share to 58%.

For an installed sale, the proposed price is $6.4 million, collected 30% at order, 30% at factory acceptance, 30% at commissioning, and 10% after the 120-day run. Direct cost is $2.15 million of equipment, $1.25 million for the EPC, $550,000 of interconnection equipment, $350,000 for certification and commissioning, and a $250,000 warranty reserve. The order deposit limits BlueBerth's peak working-capital exposure to $1.4 million. Annual controls and support would add $180,000 of revenue at $70,000 direct cost.

For charging as a service, a project SPV would spend $5.1 million before contingency and charge $0.34 per kWh on a 10-year, 9 GWh-per-year take-or-pay contract. Grid energy passed through to the customer costs $0.14 per kWh, and direct maintenance, insurance, and network operations cost $0.035 per kWh. BlueBerth would own the customer contract and raw operating data. A lender's non-binding indication is for 70% project debt, 9% interest, and 1.35 minimum debt-service coverage, but only after the interconnection agreement and the 120-day reliability gate; before then the debt is unavailable.

The incumbent EPC instead offers BlueBerth $500,000 at commissioning plus a $150,000 annual controls license per berth. BlueBerth's direct integration cost would be $80,000 initially and $45,000 per year. The EPC would own the customer contract, provide BlueBerth only anonymized monthly summaries, and demands five-year West Coast exclusivity. It can deliver four berths per year. Two alternate EPCs are technically capable but would each take nine months and $160,000 to qualify. Building construction internally would require $900,000 of tools, seven hires costing $1.8 million per year, and six extra months before the first site; after the third simultaneous site it is forecast to save 12% of the current $1.25 million EPC price. Only the Sound Crossing site is currently funded.

The founders will take conventional venture equity only if the corporate business can credibly reach $100 million of annual recurring gross profit within eight years; otherwise they prefer a durable company growing 20-30% annually with customer and project financing. The reachable ferry-berth market supplied for this decision is 48 berths over eight years, each assumed to have the same 9 GWh volume. Do not credit tugboats, cargo ports, carbon credits, or cost declines without new evidence. A VC has expressed non-binding interest in investing $20 million if the $100 million path is shown; it has not offered cash or terms.

The board authorizes at most $250,000 for a decision test, no long-lead equipment orders, no construction hires, and no exclusivity. By August 1, BlueBerth can put both the $6.4 million sale and a service offer in front of Sound Crossing. The utility will return a binding interconnection price and schedule by September 30. Sound Crossing will choose or reject both offers by October 15. For a sale, it can wire the 30% deposit at signing. For service, it will sign only at $0.32-$0.34 per kWh, at least 9 GWh per year for 10 years, and a termination payment of at least $750,000. The board will permit an SPV only with a conditional lender commitment covering at least 65% of project cost at no more than 10% interest, at least 1.35 debt-service coverage, and no more than $1.8 million of BlueBerth equity. Treat an interconnection quote at or below $750,000 and 12 months as acceptable, $750,001-$1.1 million or 13-18 months as a repair/alternate-site case, and anything worse as a stop for this berth. The EPC license is acceptable only at no less than its offered cash amounts, without geographic exclusivity, and with raw event-level operating data available to BlueBerth. If more than one route clears its gates, choose an order for them rather than pretending they can all be the first deployment.

criteria.description: Pass only if the answer names `designing-business-models` as primary, states that BlueBerth is not survival-bound, and applies the pre-deployment capital-heavy and high-harm product gates before committing to a route; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the answer records the customer, payer, contract, and data-control differences across the three routes and correctly calculates sale gross margin of $1.85 million (28.9%), service contribution of $1.485 million per year with about 3.43 years unlevered payback, and license contribution of $420,000 initially and $105,000 annually; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the answer calculates that 48 service berths yield at most $71.28 million of annual recurring contribution, recognizes that this misses the $100 million venture-equity gate, and therefore preserves the durable customer/project-financed path until reliability or expansion evidence changes the capital fit; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the answer defines one test capped at $250,000, uses the August 1, September 30, and October 15 dates, and precommits numeric sale, service-SPV, license/partner, repair, and stop branches from the supplied customer, lender, data-control, and interconnection gates, with a first-deployment tiebreak; otherwise fail.

Pass only if explicit ordered `Handoffs:` make `learning-from-users` next for customer evidence, route interfaces and field rollout to `engineering-for-leverage` then `shipping-and-iterating-products`, use `raising-and-governing-capital` only for a gated service-SPV, and defer `acquiring-and-growing-users` until stable paid deployment; otherwise fail.
